# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
22	
23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.
26	
27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
28	
29	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
30	
31	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
32	
33	A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
34	
35	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
36	
37	FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
38	
39	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the stroke being limited by the travel available to the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.
40	
41	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
42	
43	An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.
44	
45	Operation
46	
47	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
48	
49	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
50	
51	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
52	
53	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
54

1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself restored to a single, continuous element by the act of closing the clamp, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is made continuous again by the act of closing the clamp, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss being connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

1	A reusable split pipe clamp has two frame halves joined by a hinge at one end and a latch at the other. A segmented cam ring lies in an annular guide of the frame, one segment carried by each frame half. Closing the frame halves brings complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end into engagement, so the segments turn as one coupled ring. Three jaw carriages slide in radial guides, each having a follower in an oblique slot of the ring, so that latch movement driving a wedge against a ring drive face rotates the ring and advances all three carriages inwardly in synchronism until pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs remaining handle travel, and an indicator pin reports its compression. Springs retract the jaws when the latch is released.

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the stroke being limited by the travel available to the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

+The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

+The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

input.summary: The application body, claims, numeral table and five figure briefs were already drafted in full, so this turn resolved the three defects the reviewer raised and one truncated line found alongside them. Removed the sentence clause that told the reader what limits the cam-ring stroke (the inventor says only "a limited stroke" and never names a limiting element, and the added clause fought with the force-limiting-stack paragraph that follows). Rewrote the follower-constraint sentence, which had said in one breath that the follower cannot move circumferentially and that it follows a path inclined to the radial direction; it now states that the slot holds the follower at a position along the slot so that circumferential ring movement displaces the follower radially, which is what the rest of the description and claim 1 say. In the FIG. 4 brief, the latch housing and its cavity are now marked as shown schematically and the walls no longer "guide" the wedge, so no undisclosed housing/wedge connection is asserted; the wedge's up-and-down movement is likewise marked schematic. Also completed the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for numeral 16, whose line ended mid-word ("does not designate the wal"), and made "over-centre" read "over-center" to match the specification. No claim, no numeral, no other section was touched. One caution the brief asked me to state plainly: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, and per input/brief.md no prior-art search was run, so the art available to this draft is empty and may well be incomplete. The Background is written from the disclosed problem alone and contains no citations, since there is no key that could honestly be cited; if a search is later run, the Background and the claim ladder should be revisited against whatever it returns.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries its weight on one relationship the inventor calls essential: the cam ring is split with the body, one segment per frame half, and the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end engage as the halves close, so the two segments thereafter rotate as one coupled ring and a single latch input reaches all three followers. That is the coupling-by-closure limitation, and it is what a band clamp, a two-bolt saddle, or a split clamp with independently driven halves does not have. With prior_art/ empty I could not name a reference the feature clears, so I put the technical problem it solves into the Background and into the specification section 'The segmented cam ring' expressly: a side-opening clamp cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and separately driven halves lose the fixed relationship between the two sides. That explanation is now on the page ahead of any argument that needs it.

Claim 1 also recites the force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge, doing real work: after all three pads land, remaining handle travel goes into the stack instead of driving one jaw farther than its neighbours. I kept it in claim 1 rather than pushing it to a dependent because the disclosure names it as part of the essential relationship, and it is a second independent point of distinction if the coupling feature is ever met.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the indicator pin and its predetermined compression range (claims 2, 3, 11, 14), the two latch positions including the over-center position (claims 4, 12), the mounting boss (claim 8 and independent claim 10), the semicircular frame halves and the three-directions distribution (claim 9), and any statement of what bounds the stroke. Claim 1 says only 'a stroke' and 'the stroke'. Each of those is disclosed and each is a fallback worth having, but none is needed to make the clamp work or to state the invention at its broadest.

The reviewer's first two findings are correct and I applied them as written. The stroke-limiting clause was an invented mechanism: the inventor never says what bounds the stroke, and the clause implied the ring always turns the full stroke, which contradicts the very next paragraph where the stack takes up whatever travel remains once the pads land on a given pipe. Nothing in claim 1 or claim 4 depended on it, so deleting it cost no support.

The follower sentence was a genuine kinematic misstatement rather than loose wording. A path inclined to the radial direction has a circumferential component, which the radial guide forbids in the same sentence. What the oblique slot actually constrains is the follower's position along the slot; the ring's circumferential movement is what converts to radial displacement. The corrected sentence now agrees with the following sentence, with claim 1, and with FIG. 3, where the post's upper and lower sides face the sides of the opening.

The third finding is also right, on a narrower ground: the disclosure names the latch housing only as the part carrying the fixed edge against which the indicator pin is read. A three-walled cavity whose walls guide the wedge is a functional connection, not a bare outline, and every other conventional element in the five briefs (hinge, latch block, pivots, spring seats, mounting boss) is marked schematic. I marked the housing and cavity schematic and dropped the guiding function rather than deleting the cavity, because the wedge still needs somewhere to be drawn and the depiction convention must stay confined to the figure brief. The description's neutral 'a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58' was left untouched, and nothing was added to the text or claims to match the drawing.

I found one further defect the review did not list: the FIG. 4 numeral instruction for 16 ended mid-word. Left as it stood it would have reached the renderer as an unfinished instruction. I completed it in the sense the fragment was heading, pointing the callout at the latch assembly as a whole rather than at any single wall, which keeps it distinct from numeral 58 on the top wall of the same enclosure.

Independent claims sit in three statutory frames that different parties infringe: the clamp itself (claim 1), the pipe-mounted equipment assembly with a sensor, tool or conduit on the mounting boss (claim 10), which reaches the integrator who ships equipment already on a clamp, and the method of clamping (claim 13), which reaches the operator's sequence. All three trace to disclosed passages; claim 13's final step, continuing the handle into the over-center position after the pads seat, is the method-side statement of the same force-limiting relationship.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, drawn as an inner circular boundary and an outer circular boundary. The inner boundary is spaced outward from the pipe 90, leaving a visible gap between them.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left of the ring and one at the right of the ring. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle centred on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring, on the side of the block remote from the second frame half 12, so that it stands as it does in FIG. 4.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is drawn as a block that crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to the jaw carriage 30 at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the ring in the upper right region.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body, right of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body, at the bottom of the ring.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

13. A method of clamping a pipe, comprising:

opening a latch of a split pipe clamp and swinging a first frame half and a second frame half of the split pipe clamp apart about a hinge at a hinge end of the split pipe clamp, a first cam ring segment being carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment being carried by the second frame half;

placing the first frame half and the second frame half around the pipe;

closing the first frame half and the second frame half about the hinge so that complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at a latch end engage one another and couple the first cam ring segment and the second cam ring segment into a coupled ring received in an annular guide of the split pipe clamp;

moving the latch to a first position in which the first frame half and the second frame half are held around the pipe with three jaw carriages of the split pipe clamp retracted;

moving the latch toward a second, over-center position, thereby driving a wedge against a ring drive face of the coupled ring and rotating the coupled ring through a stroke;

advancing the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism by movement of a follower of each jaw carriage in a respective oblique slot of the coupled ring, until a jaw pad pivotally mounted on each jaw carriage seats on the pipe; and

continuing to move a latch handle of the latch into the second, over-center position after all three jaw pads have seated on the pipe, thereby compressing a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge rather than advancing one of the jaw carriages farther inwardly than the others.

(3) FIG-1.md now specifies a broken cutting-plane line along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, running past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, that being the viewing direction of FIG. 3; the FIG. 3 caption now locates the view by that cutting-plane line. reasoning: The FIG. 5 caption defect was a cross-reference problem, not a source problem, so the cure belonged in the caption. The alternative, drawing the boss into FIG. 1, would have put an expressly optional feature into the view that establishes the base embodiment, and the disclosure says the boss may be carried, not that it is present. Naming it 'provided with the optional mounting boss' keeps FIG. 5 an embodiment of the FIG. 1 clamp while telling the reader why the boss is absent from FIG. 1.

Claim 13's sequence error mattered because the whole force-limiting relationship depends on the pads seating before the handle finishes its travel. Reciting completed arrival at over-center and then continuing into it made the claim recite a sequence the specification contradicts, which is the kind of internal conflict that costs support later. 'Toward' in the fifth step and 'into the second, over-center position' in the last step restore the disclosed order without adding any limitation: the ring still turns through the stroke while the latch travels, and the stack still takes only the travel remaining after all three pads contact.

The suggestion called for a line labelled 3-3, but the image pipeline draws only geometry and then places the listed numerals deterministically, so a brief must never ask it to render characters. I specified the line, its extent, and the arrow direction as geometry, stated that it carries no drawing text, and wrote the FIG. 3 caption to locate the view by that cutting-plane line rather than by a 3-3 designation. The reader gets the indication the finding asked for and the caption and the sheet agree.

The arrows are specified as both pointing to the same side of the line, that side being the viewing direction of FIG. 3. That is the physically correct indication for a plane containing the carriage's radial direction and the frame axis: the viewing direction is perpendicular to that plane, so both arrows point circumferentially to one side, and stating it once avoids an arrow pair that contradicts the section it labels.

To make room under the character limit I cut only renderer instructions, never geometry or relationships. 'Leaving a visible gap between them' restated the spacing already given by 'spaced outward from the pipe 90'. 'So that it stands as it does in FIG. 4' told the renderer to match another sheet rather than describing the lever, and the lever's position is already fixed by the side of the block it extends from. The three numeral endpoints lost narrowing modifiers such as 'right of the topmost jaw carriage' and 'at the bottom of the ring' and now name broad interior targets, which is what the endpoint guidance asks for; the endpoints that must stay discriminating, notably 30 and 40 on the topmost carriage and 16 on the latch block, kept the wording that distinguishes them from neighbouring parts.

Nothing in the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments was changed to accommodate anything a renderer produced. The only claim edit was the sequence correction, which flows from the specification and the disclosure, and the only figure edits were the cutting-plane line and the removal of invented rendering constraints.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle centred on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is drawn as a block that crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. Each end of the line is designated by the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow at that end, so that the plane reads as line 3-3. That section designation is not a reference numeral and designates no part.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the ring at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The flat plate is a spring seat, and the latch housing, its cavity, and the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes are shown schematically.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section carries the parts shown; a channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, and the frame is broken away above the band, exposing its upper side. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body in section, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the lower cavity between the left and right walls, its up-and-down movement shown schematically. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag compression spring line from the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate at a point spaced from the pivot. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the flat plate through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it.

input.summary: Fixed all four findings. (1) The directional-terms paragraph in draft/08-detailed-description.md no longer says the frame axis is the axis with which a clamped pipe's axis substantially coincides; it now defines the frame axis solely as the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, and no centering statement was added anywhere else. I checked the rest of the body text for the same assertion; that clause was the only occurrence, and no claim recited centering, so nothing else moved. (2) The FIG. 4 brief now specifies a workable drive train: the latch handle 50 is pivoted at the upper right of the cavity, a short arm reaches from the pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate at a point spaced from the pivot, and the lever runs from the pivot up and to the right out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, ending inside the drawing area and leaning right past the upright in the over-center position. The view paragraph now marks the latch housing, its cavity, and that gap as shown schematically. Handle travel therefore reaches the plate, the spring stack 54, and the wedge 52, and the lever leaves the housing through a specified opening instead of through solid material; the indicator pin 56 still rises from the plate through its own hole in the top wall. (3) FIG-1.md now designates each end of the cutting-plane line with the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow at that end so the plane reads as line 3-3, and states that the designation is not a reference numeral; numeral 3 was not added to the numeral list or to draft/numerals.md, since it designates no part. The FIG. 3 caption in draft/07-drawings.md and the FIG. 3 sentence in the detailed description now both locate the view as taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. (4) The FIG. 4 entry for numeral 16 now places the numeral in free space just outside the lower right of the enclosure with a straight lead line ending in an arrowhead directed at the latch assembly as a whole, so the lead line ends on the assembly it designates instead of in empty space. Both edited briefs needed room: I trimmed only invented rendering constraints, not disclosed geometry or relationships. FIG-1.md is 2793 characters and FIG-4.md is 2797, with every other brief unchanged and under the limit. The numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims, and all five figure briefs are in step.
reasoning: The coaxiality clause was the one place where the draft claimed a result rather than a structure. The disclosure says the carriages are distributed around the closed frame and that the slots give synchronized inward travel; synchronized travel from an unspecified distribution does not put the pipe on the frame axis, and the figure brief itself marks the carriage spacing as a depiction convention. Deleting the clause cost no claim support, because no claim recites centering, and the definitional paragraph still does its only necessary job of fixing what inward, outward, and circumferential mean.

I left the title as supplied in input/brief.md and added nothing to the text to justify it. A title is a filing formality and carries no technical assertion; importing a centering statement into the description to match it would have been the reverse of the correct authority order.

The FIG. 4 defects were kinematic, not cosmetic, and FIG. 4 is the sheet whose stated purpose is showing the drive train. A lever with nothing on the far side of its pivot cannot displace the plate below it, so as previously specified no handle travel would have reached the spring stack or the wedge, and the sheet would have contradicted the force-limiting relationship that claim 1 and claim 13 rest on. Adding the short arm on the far side of the pivot makes the depicted train do what the text requires: plate down, stack compressed, wedge down, band driven left along the ring drive face 36.

The exit path was the second half of the same problem. The top wall has to stay intact because the indicator pin 56 passes through a hole in it, and that pin reading against a fixed edge of the housing is disclosed subject matter. Rather than open the top wall or move the pin, I gave the lever a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and marked the housing, cavity, and gap as schematic. The housing's wall arrangement stays a depiction convention confined to the figure brief, which is what the earlier review required, and nothing about it entered the description or the claims.

On the cutting-plane designation I had previously kept the line free of text because the geometry image renders no characters. The formality is a real requirement, so the designation is now specified in the brief and the caption uses the customary line 3-3 form. I deliberately did not add 3 to the numeral list or to draft/numerals.md: a section-line designation names a view, not a part, and putting it in the table would break the one-numeral-one-part rule that every other entry obeys. Saying in the brief that the designation is not a reference numeral keeps the two systems distinct for anyone auditing the sheet.

For numeral 16 the fix is the arrowhead, not a new endpoint. The latch is an assembly, and pointing the lead line at any single wall would have designated the housing 58, which already has its own endpoint on the top wall hatching. A straight lead line ending in an arrowhead directed at the assembly is the recognized way to designate the whole thing, and it removes the lead line that previously ended in empty space.

Both edited briefs went over the length limit once the substantive additions were in, so the trimming had to come out of rendering instructions. I removed the redundant no-shading control, the in-section qualifier on a body already established as sectioned, the compression qualifier on a spring line already drawn as a zigzag, the second statement that the numeral 16 lies inside the drawing area, and the instruction that the latch lever be positioned relative to the second frame half 12, which was a renderer constraint with no disclosure behind it. Every physical body, contact, opening, and path that the reviewer verified as consistent across FIGS. 2, 3, and 4 is still specified, including the slot obliquity, the drive sense, and the wedge slant.

lines: FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

-The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

+The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the flat plate spring seat, the latch housing and its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, the linkage by which the latch handle 50 acts on the flat plate, and the coupling of the indicator pin 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 54.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band so that its upper side is exposed. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the lower cavity between the left and right walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line from the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short schematic arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 to stand above it.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16 latch: place the numeral in free space just outside the lower right of the enclosure, with a straight lead line ending in an arrowhead directed at the latch assembly as a whole.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the band at the left.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34; the depth of the opening is shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line acting between the jaw carriage 30 and the wall of the channel so as to urge the jaw carriage 30 upward, that is, radially outward; its seats are shown schematically. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. Each end of the line is designated by the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow at that end, so that the plane reads as line 3-3. That designation is not a reference numeral.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the flat plate spring seat, the latch housing and its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, the linkage by which the latch handle 50 acts on the flat plate, and the coupling of the indicator pin 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 54.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band so that its upper side is exposed. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the lower cavity between the left and right walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line from the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short schematic arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 to stand above it.

- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the flat plate spring seat, the latch housing and its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, the linkage by which it acts on the flat plate, and the coupling of the indicator pin 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 54.

At the lower left a plain hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band, exposing its upper side. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between the left and right walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line from the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short schematic arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate. From the pivot the lever runs up and to the right, out through a gap between the right end of the top wall and the upper end of the right wall, and ends inside the drawing area, leaning right past the upright in the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it.

- 16 latch: place the numeral in free space just outside the lower right of the enclosure, with a straight lead line ending in an arrowhead directed at the latch assembly as a whole.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the band at the left.

- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.

- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left and one at the right. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block outward and away from the ring.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12. The circumferential positions of the three jaw carriages 30, and their apportionment between the two frame halves, are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90; the depth of that arc is shown schematically. That member is the jaw pad 40.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the ring at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3. Each end of the line is designated by the view number of FIG. 3, placed outside the arrow, so that the plane reads as line 3-3; that designation is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the ring at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage's inner end.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

content.text: All six findings are fixed and every brief is within the length limit.

input.summary: Fixed all six findings. (1) The indicator pin in figures/FIG-4.md no longer rises from the handle-driven spring seat; it rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it, so its position relative to the housing follows stack compression as the description and claims 2, 3, 11, and 14 require, and its coupling to the stack is listed as schematic. (2) The handle-to-spring-seat linkage is now expressly a depiction convention: the schematic list in the view paragraph covers the linkage by which the latch handle 50 acts on the flat plate, the short arm is described as a short schematic arm, and the lever-ratio wording "at a point spaced from the pivot" is gone, so the brief fixes no force ratio. (3) The FIG. 4 annular-guide muddle is resolved: the plain hatched body simply holds the cam ring band, with the frame broken away above the band to expose its upper side, which agrees with the groove bounded above and below in FIGS. 3 and 5 and removes the channel-in-the-upper-face contradiction. (4) The inferred retracted state is out of the claims and the description: claims 4 and 12 now recite the first position as holding the halves closed around the pipe without the pipe being clamped, claim 13 recites the same for its first-position step, and draft/08-detailed-description.md now says the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. Removing that phrase from claim 13 took the antecedent for "the three jaw carriages" with it, so the advancing step now introduces "three jaw carriages of the split pipe clamp" and the antecedent basis in that step, in the final step, and in claim 15 is intact. The retraction statements that remain in the description describe the released condition, which the disclosure states directly. (5) The jaw pad face in FIG-1.md is now a concave arc whose depth is shown schematically, matching FIG. 3's unqualified concave arc. (6) FIGS. 3 and 5 no longer fix the annular guide groove as wider than deep; both now mark its proportions as shown schematically. Room for the additions came only from rendering-only wording, never from disclosed geometry: FIG-1.md is 2798 characters, FIG-3.md 2605, FIG-4.md 2791, FIG-5.md 1579, and FIG-2.md is unchanged at 2658. The numeral table was not touched, no numeral was added or removed, and the drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims, and all five briefs remain synchronized.
reasoning: The indicator pin defect was the one that would have broken the invention on the page. With the pin on the plate and the plate's height set by a rigid housing-mounted handle, plate height reports handle angle, so nothing the spring stack did could move the pin against the fixed housing edge. Taking the pin off the plate and coupling it to the stack restores the reading the disclosure states: the pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters the predetermined compression range. I did not touch the description or claims 2, 3, 11, or 14, because they already said the right thing; the brief was what disagreed with them.

The linkage finding is about substance leaking into a drawing convention. 'At a point spaced from the pivot' fixes a lever ratio, and a lever ratio is how much force the handle delivers to the stack, which the disclosure never specifies. I deleted the phrase outright rather than merely labelling it, and then also put the linkage in the schematic list, so neither the geometry nor its mechanical advantage can be read as disclosed. The one thing the brief still asserts is that handle movement presses the plate down, which is the disclosed relationship that the stack lies between the handle and the wedge.

I consolidated all the depiction conventions for this sheet into a single schematic list in the view paragraph rather than scattering markings through the text. That covers the spring seat, the housing and cavity, the handle exit gap, the handle-to-plate linkage, and the pin-to-stack coupling in one place a reader can check, and it freed the characters the substantive additions needed. The wedge no longer carries its own movement marking because nothing in the brief now attributes a guiding function to the walls; it is described only as lying in the cavity between them, and the cavity is schematic.

The FIG. 4 annular-guide wording had to be reconciled across three sheets, not just fixed locally. FIGS. 3 and 5 both show the guide as a groove with frame material above and below the ring, open in the axial direction. Saying in FIG. 4 that the ring sits in a channel in the upper face contradicted that, and also contradicted the broken-away frame in the same sentence. The body now simply holds the band with the frame broken away above it, which is what a fragmentary view of that same groove looks like from the axial direction and leaves one depiction of the guide serving all three figures.

On the retracted-jaws point, the disclosure states the outward bias only for the released latch, and characterises the first position only as holding the halves around the pipe without clamping. Reciting the retracted state in three claims added an unstated condition that an examiner could read as a structural requirement on the first position and that would have to be argued from silence. 'Without the pipe being clamped' says exactly what the source says and, being broader, gives up nothing.

Removing that phrase from claim 13 created an antecedent problem, because the retracted-carriages recitation was where 'three jaw carriages' first appeared. I moved the introduction to the advancing step rather than reinstating the phrase, so the method now introduces the carriages where it first acts on them, and the later references in that step, in the final step, and in claim 15 all trace back to it.

The two proportion findings were about drawings asserting dimensions the inventor never gave. (3) The FIG. 4 annular-guide muddle is resolved: the plain hatched body simply holds the cam ring band, with the frame broken away above the band to expose its upper side, which agrees with the groove bounded above and below in FIGS. 3 and 5 and removes the channel-in-the-upper-face contradiction. (4) The inferred retracted state is out of the claims and the description: claims 4 and 12 now recite the first position as holding the halves closed around the pipe without the pipe being clamped, claim 13 recites the same for its first-position step, and draft/08-detailed-description.md now says the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30.
